qs.q: The gold standard for diagnosing osteoporosis is ---
qs.e: DEXA scan measures bone mineral density and is the established gold standard for diagnosing osteoporosis.

o: T-score between minus one and minus two point five
Elevated bone turnover markers measured in serum
Bone mineral density T-score less than or equal to minus two point five
Any fragility fracture occurring after age fifty years
qs.e: WHO definition: T-score compares BMD to young adult mean. Normal: T ≥ −1.0. Osteopenia: −1.0 to −2.5. Osteoporosis: ≤ −2.5. Severe osteoporosis: ≤ −2.5 + fragility fracture. DEXA scan is gold standard. FRAX tool calculates 10-year fracture probability. Treatment: bisphosphonates (alendronate), denosumab, teriparatide (severe cases).

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease with low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration, raising fracture risk. Diagnosis relies on bone mineral density and clinical risk factors.

sections.p: Osteoporosis is defined by a bone mineral density (BMD) T‑score ≤ ‑2.5 at the lumbar spine, hip, or forearm, or by a fragility fracture in the presence of low BMD.
b: BMD measured by DXA is the gold standard
Fracture history can diagnose even if DXA unavailable

t.b: What is the bone density? – A T‑score ≤ ‑2.5 confirms osteoporosis; ‑1 to ‑2.5 indicates osteopenia.

sections.p: Severity is staged by BMD T‑score and presence of fractures: osteopenia (‑1 to ‑2.5), osteoporosis (≤ ‑2.5), severe/established osteoporosis (≤ ‑2.5 with fragility fracture).
b: Fracture history upgrades severity
FRAX 10‑year risk >20% for major osteoporotic fracture is high risk

sections.p: Most cases are primary: post‑menopausal estrogen loss and age‑related bone loss. Secondary causes must be screened, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Post‑menopausal estrogen deficiency
Age‑related senile bone loss
Chronic glucocorticoid use
Malabsorption (celiac, inflammatory bowel disease)
HIV infection or antiretroviral therapy
Chronic TB or vertebral TB causing localized loss
Rheumatic diseases with long‑term steroids

sections.p: Patients are often asymptomatic until a low‑impact fracture occurs, commonly at the vertebrae, hip, or distal radius.
b: Back pain from vertebral compression fracture
Loss of height or kyphosis
Hip pain after a fall from standing height

sections.p: Investigations confirm low bone density, assess fracture risk, and look for secondary causes.

t.b: Are bone turnover markers abnormal? – Normal calcium with high ALP may suggest high turnover disease.
Is vitamin D deficient? – <20 ng/mL indicates deficiency, which worsens bone loss.
Is hyperthyroidism present? – Low TSH can accelerate bone loss.
Is HIV infection a contributor? – HIV and some antiretrovirals increase fracture risk.

sections.p: Complications include painful vertebral fractures, hip fractures, and secondary spinal cord compression.
b: Sudden back pain with height loss – possible vertebral fracture
Inability to bear weight after a fall – possible hip fracture
Progressive kyphosis causing respiratory compromise

sections.p: Treat underlying causes, ensure adequate calcium/vitamin D, and start anti‑resorptive therapy. Lifestyle measures support bone health.
b: Calcium 1000‑1200 mg/day from diet or supplements
Vitamin D 800‑1000 IU/day (or higher if deficient)
Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) – inhibit osteoclasts, reduce fracture risk
Denosumab for renal impairment or intolerance to bisphosphonates – RANKL inhibitor
Avoid long‑term steroids if possible; switch to steroid‑sparing agents

sections.p: Re‑measure BMD every 1‑2 years, monitor adherence, and reinforce fall‑prevention strategies.
b: DXA repeat at 2 years if on therapy, sooner if fracture occurs
Assess fall risk: vision, home hazards, muscle strength
Encourage weight‑bearing exercise (walking, resistance training)

sections.p: Conditions that also cause bone pain or fractures can be mistaken for osteoporosis.
b: Osteomalacia – low vitamin D causing soft bones, labs show low calcium/phosphate
Paget disease – focal bone enlargement, high ALP
Metastatic bone disease – lytic lesions on imaging

sections.p: Certain factors may mask true bone health.
b: Obesity can give falsely high BMD despite poor bone quality
Degenerative spinal changes can overestimate lumbar spine BMD
Recent vertebral fracture may lower BMD, exaggerating severity

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe back pain after a minor fall
Inability to stand or walk after a fall
Progressive loss of height or new kyphosis

faq.a: Yes, especially after age 70 or with risk factors like steroids, low testosterone, or chronic disease.

faq.q: Is calcium alone enough to prevent fractures?
faq.a: No, calcium must be combined with vitamin D and, when indicated, anti‑resorptive medication.
They have strong evidence for reducing vertebral and hip fractures and are inexpensive.
